content_units: Here are the metrics that matter most from your 4-month dataset across North and South.
-   Ad Cost per Order (CPO)   = Ad Spend / Orders
Segment   Revenue   Orders   Ad Spend   AOV   CPO   ROAS
1) Revenue trend by month and region
- Shows that   North leads every month  , but South narrows the gap in April.
- Makes month-to-month changes easy to spot.
- Best format:   2-line chart   with month on x-axis and revenue on y-axis.
- Revenue alone can hide efficiency; ROAS shows how well ad spend converts into sales.
- South is weaker in February, then improves sharply by April.
3) Orders vs ad spend by region/month
- Helps you see whether more spend is actually generating more orders.
- Useful for identifying whether one region is buying growth too expensively.
- Best format:   scatter plot   with ad spend on x-axis and orders on y-axis, colored by region.
- North has a steadier spend-to-orders relationship.
- South’s February point likely stands out as   less efficient   than the others.
-   AOV is almost identical   across regions:
- That means the revenue gap is mostly driven by   order volume  , not basket size.
- South improves late in the period and actually posts   slightly better ROAS than North in April  .
- North contributed about   53.6% of total revenue
- South contributed about   46.4% of total revenue
- North contributed about   54.0% of total orders
1) North is the stronger engine, but South is catching up
North consistently brings in more revenue and more orders, and it does so with better ad efficiency overall. But South rebounds well after February and closes the revenue gap by April.
2) February is the main warning month
South declines in both revenue and orders in February even though ad spend rises versus January. That is the clearest sign of underperforming marketing or weaker conversion that month.
3) Basket size is not the problem
Both regions have nearly the same AOV, so customers are spending about the same per order. If you want more revenue, the main lever is   more orders  , not necessarily higher price per order.
That suggests something started working better in March-April: campaign quality, targeting, seasonality, or sales execution.
5) North may be nearing a short-term plateau
North grows strongly through March, then dips in April:
This does not look like a collapse, but it does suggest North should be monitored for saturation or reduced marginal return on ad spend.
